newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian power de-regulation calms price swings.
newsitem.headline: Australian power de-regulation calms price swings.

text.p: Extreme volatility in Australian electricity prices has partly subsided since the introduction of the first phase of a de-regulated national electricity market in early May, an industry conference was told on Wednesday.

Electricity prices have also fallen in the two main eastern states of New South Wales (NSW) and Victoria since they were linked in March into what is called the National Electricity Market 1 (NEM1), the conference was also told.

But low NEM1 average prices of around A$18 a megawatt hour (MWh) still sporadically jump to A$70 or even A$100 a MWh, mainly under the influence of demand surges and the output response of generators, a Gas and Electricity Risk Management conference was told.

As markets gear for more widespread trading in a range of contract-based power products, Australian electricity prices remain far more volatile than other traded financial implements, conference figures showed.

Electricity prices still jump by 300 percent or more in a matter of minutes, against price variations of less than 50 percent by other commodities, equities and, the most stable of all, bonds, Sandy Wilkinson, head of energy at merchant bank RMB Australia, said.
"It's not a rational market ... it's an immature market," he said.
Australian electricity's very volatility, however, forms the basis for the growing market in traded electricity and derivative financial products.
The Sydney Futures Exchange plans to start trading electricity futures in September.

Conference figures show that Victorian electricity prices, which earlier this year showed regular wild swings between nil and about A$70 a MWh, stabilised from the beginning of May to move between a band of about A$10 and A$30 a MWh.
With Victoria regularly drawing electricity from NSW through NEM1, Victorian prices have fallen into line with traditionally more-stable prices in NSW.
Figures also showed a gentle easing of prices overall since May, from about A$20 a MWh.
"There is no doubt that (Victoria/NSW) prices have now converged," Lloyd Holmes, general manager market development operations of government-owned Victorian Power Exchange, said.
Holmes, however, told Reuters that accurate quantification of price declines was virtually impossible.
While daily averages were down, Victorian prices under NEM1 tended to be higher overnight and lower during daytime, while NSW prices tended to be lower overnight and higher during daytime.
Victorian prices also reflected change in the seasons much more than in NSW, he said.
Holmes declined to say whether de-regulation would bring lower electricity prices in the longer-term.
"Different parts of the industry have different views," he said. "Some say these (present) prices are non-sustainable."

David Coddington, managing consultant energy and utilities of EDS Australia, sees "low" pool prices in the longer-term as part of a cycle of mothballing of plant at low prices, retirement of ageing plant, followed by investment, then over-investment and the beginning of the cycle again.
Coddington sees prices remaining low in the short-term.
As demand equalises, generators will later be in a position to set "take it or leave it" prices, he said.
